question: Why did chemists take 44 years to notice that one rare-earth 'element' was really two?
answer: Because the rare earths are chemical near-copies. Carl Mosander named didymium, the twin, in 1841; only in 1885 did Carl Auer von Welsbach split it into praseodymium and neodymium, by crystallising its salts over and over. Refiners still face the same sameness: separation plants run the liquid through hundreds of extraction tanks in series.
move: When two things behave identically, expect them to be counted as one.
reference: Emsley, Nature's Building Blocks: An A-Z Guide to the Elements, 2nd edition, Oxford University Press, 2011
